The central question is: when you chain models of increasing capability (a fast/cheap gatekeeper that either answers or escalates to a slower/expensive oracle), does the system's Pareto frontier of latency vs. accuracy degrade over time if the incoming query difficulty distribution shifts — and by how much, under what conditions, is that degradation unrecoverable without retraining? The key concepts are the routing threshold (the score at which the gatekeeper escalates), the difficulty distribution (how hard queries actually are at inference time vs. at routing-policy design time), and the Pareto frontier itself (the set of threshold settings where you can't improve accuracy without worsening latency or vice versa). The cascade lives or dies on one critical assumption a beginner ignores: that the gatekeeper's confidence scores are calibrated proxies for actual difficulty, and non-stationarity attacks precisely this — if the world shifts so that what the gatekeeper calls "easy" now has a systematically different error rate, the routing policy is silently wrong without any alarm firing. An expert also worries about asymmetric drift: query difficulty can shift in ways that are invisible to the gatekeeper's feature space (e.g., new jargon, domain shift in a subpopulation) while aggregate metrics like average latency stay flat, masking accuracy collapse on the shifted slice. The deeper trap is that escalation rates — the observable you'd use to detect drift — can stay constant even as the composition of what gets escalated changes, so standard monitoring gives false comfort.

Lowering the escalation threshold is a blunt instrument that treats the symptom — too many hard queries retained — without addressing the cause, which is that the gatekeeper's difficulty signal has become miscalibrated on the shifted subdistribution. If drift is localized (e.g., a new query topic or user cohort), blanket threshold reduction escalates a flood of still-easy queries alongside the newly-hard ones, wasting oracle capacity and potentially saturating it, which in a real serving system means queueing latency spikes that eliminate the budget you thought you had. The correct remediation hierarchy starts with router recalibration: using the labeled drift sample to re-fit the threshold or re-weight the gatekeeper's confidence scores on the affected slice, which is what Desai and Durrett (2020) do with temperature scaling on NLI cascades to restore calibration without retraining. If the drift is structural — the gatekeeper lacks features to distinguish the new hard queries at all — recalibration fails and you need router fine-tuning or feature augmentation on the drifted slice, which requires a labeled buffer large enough to avoid catastrophic forgetting on the original distribution; LoRA-style updates (Hu et al., 2022) are practical here precisely because they limit parameter movement. A subtler failure mode: if the oracle itself has degraded on the new distribution (plausible when both models share a pretraining corpus that's now stale), escalating more queries just moves errors upstream rather than fixing them, so remediation must first establish whether the oracle's conditional accuracy on the drifted slice is actually high enough to justify the escalation cost. The correct monitoring primitive is therefore a three-way conditional accuracy table — (retained∩correct, retained∩wrong, escalated∩correct, escalated∩wrong) — tracked separately on the drifted slice, which tells you whether the problem is router miscalibration, oracle inadequacy, or both.

For fastest router recovery, you want annotations that maximally shift the decision boundary, which means querying near the current escalation threshold — classic margin sampling — but restricted to the drifted slice, because examples far from the boundary carry little gradient signal for recalibration. Settles (2009) established this for active learning generally, but the cascade context adds a constraint: you specifically want threshold-proximal examples where the gatekeeper's confidence is high (it would retain) yet self-consistency variance is also high (internal disagreement suggests miscalibration), a conjunction that Kadavath et al.'s "know what you don't know" framing operationalizes as a cheap pre-annotation filter. For tightest accuracy bound on the current system, the objective flips — you need a statistically representative sample of the retained population to estimate conditional error rate with tight confidence intervals, which means stratified random sampling over the drifted slice regardless of proximity to the threshold, because margin sampling is biased and will give you a distorted picture of the actual error rate distribution. These two objectives are genuinely in tension: the margin sample is informationally efficient for repair but produces a biased accuracy estimate; the random sample gives you an honest bound but wastes annotation budget on easy examples that don't move the router. The practical resolution used in production systems like Google's Vizier and described in Sculley et al.'s 2015 "Hidden Technical Debt" paper is a batched hybrid: allocate roughly 70% of annotation budget to margin/uncertainty sampling for recovery and 30% to stratified random for monitoring, then update both the router and the accuracy estimate simultaneously — the split ratio itself should be tuned to how far outside SLA the current accuracy bound sits.

The obvious fallback is full escalation — route everything to the oracle during the remediation window — and it does protect the accuracy floor, but its hidden costs are severe and compounding. Oracle throughput is sized for the baseline escalation rate (say 30%); suddenly routing 100% of traffic can saturate the oracle queue, introducing tail latencies that themselves violate SLA on the latency side, and in cloud deployments trigger autoscaling that takes minutes to stabilize, meaning the first 5-15 minutes of "safe" fallback are actually the most dangerous. The second hidden cost is distribution contamination: if the oracle's outputs during the fallback window are used as pseudo-labels for router retraining (a tempting shortcut), you're now training on oracle errors on the drifted slice, which can be systematically wrong in the same direction, baking the oracle's blind spots into the router permanently. The correct policy is tiered escalation with load shedding: immediately lower the threshold to escalate the high-uncertainty drifted-slice queries specifically (using the self-consistency filter as a cheap runtime classifier), while shedding or queuing low-priority requests to keep oracle utilization below saturation — this is the approach Crankshaw et al.'s Clipper serving system (2017) used for model fallback under SLA constraints, prioritizing p99 latency preservation over throughput. A subtler but critical hidden cost of full escalation is masking the drift signal itself: once you stop routing anything to the gatekeeper, you lose the conditional accuracy stream on retained queries, so you can no longer measure whether your router recalibration is actually working, effectively going blind during the window when visibility matters most.

The correct ramp protocol is stratified shadow scoring: before restoring any live routing decisions to the repaired router, run it in parallel on live traffic — logging its decisions without acting on them — and compare its retain/escalate decisions against the fallback oracle's outputs as a noisy ground-truth proxy, slice by slice across query features. A time-based ramp is dangerous because held-out validation accuracy is clean on the labeled drifted slice, which is a biased sample — it was collected by the active learning loop specifically around the decision boundary and the detected drift cluster, so it systematically underrepresents novel drift modes that weren't yet visible when annotation occurred. This is a version of Goodhart's Law applied to recalibration: the metric you optimized (validation accuracy on the labeled drift sample) is no longer a reliable proxy for the true objective (accuracy on the live drifted distribution) the moment the live distribution continues evolving during the annotation window. The practical safeguard is a canary gate with a sequential probability ratio test (SPRT): route a small fixed fraction (e.g., 5%) through the repaired router, and use Wald's SPRT to decide at each batch whether the conditional error rate on retained queries is statistically consistent with the pre-drift baseline — SPRT is optimal here because it minimizes expected samples to a decision under both null and alternative, which Johari et al.'s 2015 "always valid inference" work extends to the continuous monitoring case. The hidden danger in even a careful ramp is ramp-induced feedback: as you shift traffic back to the router, oracle load drops, latency improves, and engineering teams feel pressure to accelerate the ramp — institutionalizing a social dynamic where the statistical stopping criterion gets overridden by operational impatience precisely when the system is most fragile.

When both models update continuously, the recalibration target is itself a moving object — you are trying to re-align the router to an oracle whose decision surface is shifting, so the standard protocol of "label a batch, retrain router, validate, ramp" breaks down because the oracle you validated against may no longer exist by the time the ramp completes. The new primitive you need is joint versioning with compatibility contracts: each router checkpoint must be tagged to a specific oracle version range it was calibrated against, and the serving system must enforce that a router trained on oracle-v12 is never paired with oracle-v15 without an intervening compatibility check — this is analogous to API versioning but for learned behavior, and almost no production systems implement it explicitly, which is why Shankar et al.'s 2022 "Operationalizing Machine Learning" survey lists model interaction bugs as among the hardest to detect in practice. The new failure mode that doesn't exist in the static case is co-adaptation drift: when both models update from overlapping data pipelines or shared feedback loops, they can converge to a mutually consistent but globally wrong equilibrium — the router learns to escalate exactly what the current oracle handles well, the oracle gets fine-tuned on what it receives, and both metrics look healthy while the jointly-unreachable query space (hard queries the router confidently retains) accumulates silent errors with no signal. The ramp protocol must therefore add a cross-version shadow test: before any live traffic shift, run the candidate router against a frozen oracle snapshot and the current oracle, and flag cases where routing decisions diverge between the two oracle versions, because those divergences are the leading indicator of co-adaptation. Concretely, Google's Sibyl system and the broader literature on reinforcement learning from human feedback both show that reward model drift and policy drift interact multiplicatively — a 5% shift in each can produce 20%+ degradation in joint behavior — which means monitoring each model's marginal metrics is insufficient and you must instrument the joint decision distribution as a first-class observable.

The minimal sufficient set has three components, each catching a failure mode the others miss. First, escalation decision entropy over time: if the router's escalate/retain distribution is collapsing — fewer and fewer query types getting escalated, tighter clustering in feature space — that's a signature of co-adaptation even before accuracy degrades, because a healthy router should maintain diverse escalation patterns as the query distribution shifts; you can measure this without labels using the entropy of router confidence scores binned by query embedding clusters. Second, oracle disagreement rate on a frozen reference set: maintain a small static probe set (500-1000 queries) labeled at system initialization, run the oracle against it on every update cycle, and track how its output distribution shifts — this is cheap, label-free after initial cost, and catches oracle drift independently of the router; Liang et al.'s HELM benchmark (2022) essentially operationalizes this idea at evaluation time, but it needs to run continuously in production. Third, and most non-obvious, retry and reformulation rate from downstream systems or users: when the cascade produces wrong answers on jointly-unreachable queries, users or calling systems often implicitly signal this through re-queries, rephrasing, or fallback invocations — this behavioral signal requires no labels and directly measures the failure consequence rather than a proxy, and Sculley et al.'s hidden technical debt framing would classify ignoring it as a monitoring anti-pattern. The combination works because entropy collapse catches the structural problem early, oracle probe drift catches unilateral oracle movement, and retry rate catches the joint failure that slips through both — any single observable alone is gameable or blind to one failure axis. Concretely, if escalation entropy drops more than one standard deviation from its 30-day baseline and retry rate rises more than 10% above baseline simultaneously, that conjunction is a near-certain indicator of co-adaptation without requiring a single new label.
